CI phases

scripts/ci.mjs

In call order, read out of main(). A fast phase also runs on --fast and in the pre-push hook; the rest only on a full run.

01
hygienefast

Everything here is about the difference between THIS working copy and a fresh clone.

02
lintfast

Biome over the whole tree with the rule set apps extend (biome.json at the root extends @frontierjs/config), warnings failing too: a warning this phase tolerated is a count that grows until someone raises the bar.

03
structurefast

The architecture rules, run over this repo's own apps and packages with the same engine `fli check` gives a client app.

04
registersfast

The three registers, graded against the rules they state about themselves.

05
snapshotsfast
06
accessfast

What did this branch do to who may do what.

07
coveragefast

Skipped is not passed. The aggregate `--filter '*'` walks straight past a package with no `test` script and prints nothing at all about it.

08
registryfast
09
advisoriesfast

Dependency posture, decided the way everything else here is decided: a phase, not a bot (`IDEAS/tooling-decisions.md` 5).

10
scaffoldfast
11
typecheckfast

Two halves: the direction of the ratchet (a git question) and the count itself (each package's own script already answers that, and exits 1 above its ceiling).

12
deployfull run

`fli new` → `fli make:deploy` → `fli deploy:local`: does the deploy pipeline containerize a real app? ~30s and it needs a Docker daemon, so it sits in the full tier rather than the pre-push one.

13
mutatefull run

`litestone mutate` over each app named in scripts/mutate-baselines.json, its score held to that file's floor (FJS-D476).

14
tutorfull run

The tutorial, executed. `docs/QUICKSTART.md` §7 exited 0 on every command it named and had never once put an app on a server — a document with no compiler behind it, which is the failure every other phase here exists to prevent one realm at a time. A lesson is…

15
perffull run

What did this branch do to how long a request takes, against the base ref.

16
testsfull run

Sequential on purpose: several suites bind ports and start real servers, and interleaved output from four different runners is unreadable when one fails.

the DEVICE'S OWN DATABASE — sierra/src/resource/local-db.js, build/local-db-plugin.js, or offline: { db: … } packages/sierra: test/local-db.test.js for the seam — when it writes, when it reads, and that null means cannot answer and falls through rather than rendering as an empty list. The engine is litestone's and is proved by packages/litestone: bun run test:browser, which is the only thing that runs it over OPFS at all. What NEITHER can see is the packaging, and the packaging is where this breaks: a bundler rewrites new Worker(new URL(…, import.meta.url)) and nothing else, the wasm entry must be served as .js, and that same static signal puts the worker in every app unless the build stubs it out — each of those failed silently, with the app looking like it worked. So a change here is also cd example && bun run build, read for the shell WEIGHT — and the numbers are three, not one: 1 kB is the seam in an app that left the database off, 880 kB is example with it on, and anything near 400 means the worker is being shipped by an app that did not ask for it (FJS-D302). example: verify:shell is what grades the feature end to end, and its decisive block is the one that empties the list cache with the network already down and asks the screen again: every other assertion passes with the database absent, because a slot a load() wrote answers the same question with the same rows. Since FJS-D337 the WARM writes no such slot for a model the device kept, which the drive asserts directly. That is how orderBy: '-id' reaching SQLite unchanged — junction's wire spelling, which litestone throws on — was invisible for as long as it existed packages/sierratest/local-db.test.jspackages/litestonebun run test:browserexampleverify:shell
the DECLARED OFFLINE READ — sierra/src/resource/offline.js, offlineQuery, or anything that builds a cache key packages/sierra: test/offline-query.test.js. Every case is warmed, then offline, then read and never the warm ran, because the way this feature fails is a warm written under a key no load() looks under — which nothing about the app looks wrong for until somebody is in a basement. Two negative controls keep that honest: breaking the key turns 6 of the 13 red, and routing the warm through load() instead of find() turns exactly the the store the screen is showing is not touched case red. A change to listKey, to either side of the warm, or to when it is armed needs a case here. The warm also fills the DEVICE's tables, which is hydration, and that half is graded in test/local-db.test.js under a question the warm never asked — the only kind a cache cannot answer. Its fake device KEEPS what it is given, because one that answers reads regardless cannot tell a hydrated device from an empty one, and the sharpest test here passed against a device nothing had written to until it did. example: verify:shell is the end of it — a screen opened offline for the first time in that browser with the cache emptied, and since FJS-D337 with no slot for the warm to have written at all: what the drive waits on is the warm's own frame, tapped before the app's first script, because a fact nothing writes cannot be read back · verify:offline for the queue underneath it packages/sierratest/offline-query.test.jsexampleverify:shell

a partial unique — @@unique([cols], where: …), partialUnique, the predicate in release.js packages/litestone: test/index-predicates.test.ts — the same file as the two rows below and a third reader. The assertions that have to stay are the ones the design turns on: the soft-delete clause is ABSENT from the emitted DDL, asserted against the text because the constraint behaves identically either way until a row is deleted; a value comparison is INLINED, because SQLite refuses a bound parameter there and every behavioral test passes against DDL that never built; it does not make a relation one-to-one; and the RENAME — a database written before the uniq<table><cols> prefix carries the index under the old name, and leaving it there makes the model's own @@index over those columns a CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS against a name already taken, which SQLite answers by doing nothing (FJS-614).
